claims.text: Enhanced corrosion resistance in the steels is caused by formation of a robust, chromium-enriched passive oxide film.
The chromium-enriched passive film inhibits further metal degradation in aggressive chemical and radiation environments.
Chromium preferentially oxidizes under oxidative and corrosive conditions.
Preferential chromium oxidation forms a dense passive film.
The dense passive film acts as a barrier that reduces further metal dissolution.
The passive film remains stable under moderate radiation.
The passive film is self-repairing under moderate radiation.
Increasing the chromium content promotes formation of a continuous, well-adhered, chromium-enriched surface oxide film.
Higher-chromium steels will have a lower corrosion rate than lower-chromium steels under identical acidified-chloride, elevated-temperature, simulated-radiation conditions.
Higher-chromium steels will form a thicker chromium-based oxide layer than lower-chromium steels.
Higher-chromium steels will form a more uniform chromium-based oxide layer than lower-chromium steels.
Higher chromium content will produce greater passive-film stability than lower chromium content.
Higher-chromium steels will exhibit less mass loss over time than the lower-chromium baseline.
The proposed acid-chloride, elevated-temperature, moderate-radiation conditions represent aggressive environments encountered in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
The proposed mechanism applies within chemical aggressiveness and radiation levels typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments.
Mechanical stresses or temperatures above unspecified levels can compromise passive-film integrity.
The study can isolate chromium content by comparing high- and low-chromium specimens with equivalent microstructures, surface finishes, and processing histories.
Mass loss and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy can quantify corrosion behavior, while XPS and SEM can characterize oxide composition, thickness, and morphology.
A lack of statistically significant differences in corrosion rate or oxide-film quality between the chromium groups would falsify the hypothesis.
